extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers interested in biological and social evolution / natural philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: Explanation and argument that the production of many effects by single causes (the 'multiplication of effects') is a part-cause of biological and social evolution, illustrated across embryology, paleontology, technology, and social organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epigenesis and absence of preformed rudiments
rubrics_metrics.description: No germ (animal or vegetal) contains the slightest rudiment, trace, or indication of the future organism; development begins with repeated spontaneous fissions producing a mass of undifferentiated cells.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a premise for arguing that successive organization phases are produced by incident agencies acting on previously existing partial organizations; supports the claim that development proceeds by transformation under external influences rather than by unfolding of preformed parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplication of effects as a part-cause of evolution
rubrics_metrics.description: A single cause often generates multitudinous and ramifying effects; such multiplication of effects is a part-cause of increasing heterogeneity in organisms and assemblages of organisms over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated inductively (examples from embryology, species divergence, social change) and deducible from principles like persistence of force; claim extended from physical heterogeneity of Earth to biological and social heterogeneity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity of identical germs to produce unlike forms under different circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: The same germ may be evolved into different forms according to circumstances (e.g., sexless embryo becoming male or female; bee larva becoming worker or queen depending on food).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supports the idea that incident forces and changing conditions acting on initially similar starting points produce divergent outcomes; used to argue that transformation superinduces new changes upon prior changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Environmental and geological change drives diversification
rubrics_metrics.description: Successive modifications of physical conditions (climate, level, local differences) resulting from geological events (e.g., uplift of archipelagos) subject organisms to new sets of conditions, leading to differentiated adaptations and the branching of species into many varieties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed hypothetical example of East Indian Archipelago uplift: varied microenvironments cause subtle alterations that, over many generations and repeated upheavals, produce multiple species/varieties from original ones; dispersion increases chances of survival and cumulative heterogeneity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changes of habit and food as agents of modification
rubrics_metrics.description: Alterations in habit (behavior) or diet induced by new environments or encounters can lead to structural and functional modifications in organisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: animals encountering new predators leading to different defenses or pursuit methods; insects and animals modified by changed food sources; these habit-driven modifications can become dominant and eventually alter organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialization and division of labor increase social heterogeneity
rubrics_metrics.description: When individuals display aptitude for making particular useful articles, specialization (division of labor) arises, leading to differentiation of roles (e.g., weapon-maker) and secondary economic and social effects (barter, exchange, further specialization).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanism: practice increases skill for specialists and reduces practice for others, reinforcing differentiation; barter causes exchange of superior goods and stimulates other members to develop aptitudes; population growth and trade intensify specialization; historical trajectory illustrated from tribal craftsmen to industrial occupations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technological inventions produce manifold social effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventions (e.g., the locomotive engine) act as proximate causes that generate complex, far-reaching, and ramified social, economic, occupational, and cultural changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete chain of effects enumerated: legal/procedural steps to build railways, creation and expansion of trades (engineers, plate-layers), changes in distribution, prices, travel habits, diffusion of literature and news — all demonstrating how one innovation multiplies effects across society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale/heterogeneity of the affected area amplifies multiplicative results
rubrics_metrics.description: The wider and more heterogeneous the area over which an influence extends, the more numerous and varied the resultant effects (e.g., telegraph's slight impact on a small homogeneous island vs. multitudinous effects in England).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implies that the same cause produces disproportionately more secondary and tertiary effects when acting on a complex, populous, or interconnected society than on a small homogeneous community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Higher complexity/intelligence increases the number and range of secondary effects
rubrics_metrics.description: In minds and societies of higher grade/complexity, a single impression or change gives rise to a larger number and more varied secondary ideas, emotions, and reactions than in lower-grade systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: perception of an unknown bird elicits only superficial curiosity in a herdsman, but prompts detailed analysis, correspondence, naming, and broader scientific consequences in a naturalist or comparative anatomist; similarly, emotions develop into richer, more compound states in more developed individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persistence of force entails dispersion and qualitative differentiation of effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of the persistence of force, when a uniform incident force falls on an aggregate made of unlike parts, that force is differently modified by each part, producing dispersed and qualitatively differentiated secondary forces; hence multiplication of effects follows from basic physical principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Logical/deductive grounding for the multiplication thesis: differences in reactions to uniform forces are the objective basis for distinguishing things; the differential forces present in unlike parts must produce corresponding different reactions, leading to further transformations and cascading multiplications.
